posts.content:
The average patient admission is being managed for 13 different diagnoses at once. Today, getting the specificity right for each one depends on a clinician's memory or a retrospective query that lands in inboxes days later.  

Abridge surfaces CDI queries quietly, inline and in the note, during the encounter.

Each query is AHIMA-compliant, documented in the record, and auditable from day one—because compliance is a feature, not a task.

The result: fewer retrospective queries, faster coding, and a record that captures the full scope of the care that happened. This way, the next clinician and the ones that follow all have it right, all the way through discharge.

posts.content:
Before Abridge, when I was rounding full time as a PA in hospital medicine, I kept a laminated card in my lab coat pocket, a cheat sheet for phrasing that would make a diagnosis land the way I meant it and keep a query from coming back at me days later. Acute on chronic. Present on admission. Sepsis, not bacteremia.
 
It worked, but only when I remembered to pull it out, and only until the guidelines changed. Getting a diagnosis right came down to what I could recall and a scrap of paper in my pocket, not the system around me.
 
That's the part I keep coming back to. A typical admission involves managing >10 diagnoses, each requiring enough specificity to reflect how sick the patient actually is. CDI teams are asking exactly the right questions. They've just had to ask them at the only moment the workflow allowed, well after the case was fresh in anyone's mind.
 
Kelly McDonald, the product manager behind this work, and I sat down to talk through how we're approaching that: clinical documentation integrity brought into the workflow itself, while the patient is still admitted and the clinician is still writing the note, aligned with AHIMA compliant query guidance so the trail holds up on review.
 
The laminated card was solving a specific problem for me, but what if the problem didn't have to exist at all?

“Freeing.“ “Affirming.” “A Revolution.”

That's how clinicians describe what it feels like to practice with Abridge.

- Cognitive load is an invisible tax. Reducing it doesn't just save minutes during a visit. It frees up the mental space to think, to create, and to be present during a visit.

posts.content:
When I joined Abridge after winning Anthropic’s hackathon earlier this year, I knew firsthand that these events can change careers.

It certainly changed mine.

So one of the first things I wanted to do after joining was help create that same opportunity for others.

This weekend, we brought together nearly 200 clinicians, engineers, researchers, and builders in San Francisco to spend 12 hours asking one question:

What could agentic AI do for healthcare if we started from first principles?

The answer came in the form of 113 projects.

Teams built everything from an ambient emergency department triage agent, to identity-aware patient monitoring with continuous re-triage, to EMS-to-inpatient handoff coordination, and even models that predict physician burnout from clinical activity patterns.

But what stayed with me wasn’t any single project. It was watching clinicians and engineers who had met only hours earlier work together as if they’d been on the same team for years. Conversations moved seamlessly between agentic architectures, clinical workflows, and operational realities. You could feel that everyone in the room believed healthcare deserves better tools.

One of my favorite moments was looking around the room and realizing just how far people had traveled to be there. Participants came from 17 countries, including Poland, Belgium, the United Kingdom, India, Singapore, and South Korea, joining colleagues from across the United States because they all believed the same thing: Healthcare is one of the most important frontiers for AI.

Healthcare is also one of the hardest domains to build for. The workflows are complex, the constraints are real, and the stakes couldn’t be higher.

That’s exactly why nearly 200 incredibly talented people chose to spend a summer Saturday working on these problems.

Looking around the room, I couldn’t help but wonder how many future founders, collaborators, and careers were beginning that day—just like mine did a few months ago.

Huge thanks to everyone who made this possible: our participants, mentors, judges, and our partners at Anthropic, Lightspeed Ventures, and Cerebral Valley.

I’ll be sharing more about the finalists and winning projects over the next few days. For now, here are a few moments from a day I won’t forget.

posts.content:
The most consequential moments in medicine are often the transitions. When a patient is admitted to the hospital, when care teams change, and when a patient is discharged, maintaining continuity of care is essential, but these are also the moments when important context can be lost. The systems that manage care delivery were never designed to keep a patient’s story complete across different settings.

Yesterday at the KLAS Arch Collaborative, I had the opportunity to demo what it looks like in Abridge when that gets solved: conversation-driven intelligence for coordinated inpatient care. One platform tracks the same patient from pre-admission through outpatient follow-up, continuously updated with the latest touchpoint and the patient’s history, all accessible to the clinician who needs it next. Organized around the patient, every detail appears where and when it’s needed. Woven through it all is clinical decision support powered by EHR context, quietly underscoring every decision point along the way. It’s the layer that allows me to act as the conductor, making sure everything is in place.

This is a full circle moment for me. The exact problems I used to solve manually on the hospital floor are the ones we addressed on stage yesterday. When a patient is admitted, there’s no more manual merging of notes across systems, no more updating histories that could be months out of date, and no more missing the vital context that can directly affect care plans.

All information is organized and available where the clinician needs it, exactly when they need it, so they can be fully present with the person in front of them.

The amazing part is how simple it feels. Like good air conditioning, it just works. That’s the future clinicians and patients deserve: a workflow built with us in mind.

posts.content:
768 applications → 199 participants → 113 projects → 12 hours → 3 winners 

Introducing the winners of the first-ever Abridge x Anthropic x Lightspeed hackathon: The Future of Agentic AI in Healthcare

Winner: HomeReady by Pranay Madan

A remote-care coordinator that enables a patient or caregiver to reduce the need for routine in-person visits to free up social workers for higher-acuity needs. 

A patient or caregiver records a guided video and audio walkthrough of the home using lidar-based home-mapping leveraging Apple devices. HomeReady reviews the walkthrough, extracts structured risks (fall hazards, bathroom access issues, medication confusion, caregiver gaps, mobility barriers, missing equipment), compares findings against the patient's discharge context, prompts for clarification if needed, triages the patient into a check-in level, drafts a risk summary for the care team, and recommends next actions such as OT referral, durable medical equipment (DME), nurse call, or social work escalation.

Second place: AloraAI by Hazel W. and Swindar Zhou

An autonomous system that matches open psychiatric beds with patients in crisis. 

AloraAI listens to case manager calls and extracts data on facility bed availability, waitlists, and admission criteria. The information gathered is written into a living knowledge graph that stays current across the entire network and checks answers in real time. The case manager still runs the call and makes the decisions. The agent also references the patient’s chart, flags anything the record doesn't support, and remembers what each call revealed so the next call starts with all of the previous information instead of from scratch. 

Third place: Twiage by Kairi W. and Nupur Garg, MD, DipABLM

An agentic AI emergency department triage team.

Clinicians describe the patient in their own words and Twiage structures that information into triage logic and applies it to cases as they come in, flagging risk and urgency faster than the status quo process can manage. It streamlines triage by combining clinical judgment with fast and structured decision-making, effectively reducing wait times and alleviating congestion across a busy emergency department. 

This hackathon was a masterclass in collaboration. Clinicians and engineers from all over the world joined forces, aligned on clinical reality, and shipped 113 meaningful projects in less than a day. 

We have the drive to fix what’s broken in healthcare—not just by talking, but by building together. The transformation starts here.

In the coming weeks, we will share more standout work. Thank you to all who participated and to Cerebral Valley for partnering on this event.
